opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a common picture where people imagine AI labs are primarily racing to automate R&D, especially AI R&D, because that's where the "explosive" feedback loop supposedly lies. I'm skeptical that this reflects either where the value is or where the incentives point.

Start with social value. R&D clearly has enormous social value, much larger than what the people doing it capture. Economists have estimated for a long time that the social returns to R&D are several times the private returns, because ideas spill over. Once someone figures something out, everyone else can use it, often without paying much for it. So in a sense, R&D is among the most socially valuable activities in the economy.

But that same fact is exactly why it's not where the private money is. If you're an AI lab trying to earn revenue, you get paid in proportion to the value you can capture, and that roughly tracks what people are currently paying for labor. In the US, total R&D spending is only around two or three percent of GDP, and much of that isn't researcher wages. Meanwhile, labor compensation overall is something like half or more of GDP. So if you automate R&D workers, you're competing for a fairly small slice of the wage bill. If you automate software engineering, customer service, administrative work, the broad mass of remote cognitive jobs, the market is orders of magnitude bigger.

So there's a gap. The activity with the highest social returns per dollar is not the one with the highest private returns for whoever automates it. I'd expect labs to be pulled toward broad automation of the economy, because that's where revenue is, rather than toward narrowly automating research.

There's also a more technical point. I don't think R&D is a separable task you can automate in isolation. Much of what drives progress, especially in AI, is scaling compute, building fabs, gathering data, running large experiments. The cognitive "having ideas" part is important but often not the bottleneck. So even if you made researchers ten times more productive, you'd still be constrained by physical inputs and experimental throughput. That makes the "automate R&D first and get a software-only singularity" story less plausible to me, and it reinforces that the economically natural path is broad automation that grows the whole economy, including the capital and compute that R&D depends on.

The upshot is that I expect progress to come from AI diffusing across the economy, generating revenue, and that revenue funding much more compute and investment. That loop is, I think, what actually drives growth, and it's more gradual and broad-based than the picture of a lab quietly automating its own researchers and taking off.

r001.rationale: The response says R&D’s social returns exceed private returns because ideas spill over, so labs capture only part of its value and have weaker private incentives to automate it.

r002.rationale: It contrasts R&D broadly with larger labor markets, but does not say labs can capture more value from software R&D than from biology R&D or basic research.

r003.rationale: It says revenue from AI diffusing across the economy can fund more compute and investment, identifying financing further AI investment as a reason to favor revenue-generating activities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a fairly standard story here that I basically buy, which is that R&D has very large positive externalities. If you're a firm doing research, you capture some fraction of the value you create, but a lot of it leaks out. Other firms copy you, patents expire, the knowledge gets embedded in the general stock of what people know how to do. The classical estimates on this put the social return to R&D at something like several times the private return, so firms systematically underinvest relative to what would be optimal for society.

Now, the question is what that implies for AI labs and their incentives to automate research. And I think the first thing to notice is that the labs are a bit of a special case, because the research they're most motivated to automate is their own. If you're OpenAI or Anthropic or Google DeepMind, the thing that's most directly valuable to you is making your own AI development go faster. You capture a lot of that privately, because it compounds into a better product and a bigger lead over competitors. So for that specific kind of R&D, I don't think the externality argument tells you there's underinvestment. If anything, the incentives are very strong, maybe stronger than you'd want from a safety point of view.

Where I think the externality story bites harder is for everything else. Think about automating research in biology, or materials science, or just the long tail of engineering problems across the economy. The social value of that is enormous. But the private return to a lab from building a system that's really good at, say, running wet lab experiments is much more diffuse. You have to sell it to a lot of customers, they have to adopt it, they have to restructure how their organizations work, and then the gains show up in the economy as a whole rather than in your revenue. So you'd expect labs to be relatively less focused on that compared to how valuable it is.

And I think that's roughly what we observe. The frontier labs are very focused on coding and math and the kinds of tasks that feed back into their own capability development, partly because those are the tasks they understand and can evaluate, but also because that's where the private returns are concentrated.

The other thing I'd add is that I'm somewhat skeptical of the picture where you just automate "the researcher" as a bundle and get a big multiplier on scientific output. A lot of what makes research valuable isn't the cognitive piece in isolation. It's the experiments, the data, the institutional context, the feedback from the real world. So even if the incentive to automate R&D were perfectly aligned with the social value, I'd expect the actual gains to come more slowly and more unevenly than people sometimes imagine, because the bottlenecks move around. You speed up one part and then something else becomes the constraint.

So if I were to summarize: the incentives are strong and well aligned for AI research automating itself, weaker than socially optimal for research in the broader economy, and in both cases the realized impact depends a lot on complementary inputs that the labs don't control. Which is why I tend to think the diffusion story matters as much as the capabilities story.

r001.rationale: The response says R&D’s social value spills over to others, while labs capture less private value from research outside their own AI development, weakening their incentive to pursue it.

r002.rationale: It contrasts labs’ incentives for their own AI development and coding or math with biology research, but does not clearly state that labs capture a greater share from software R&D than from biology or basic research.

r003.rationale: The response describes private returns from better products and competitive leads, but does not identify financing further AI investment as a reason to prioritize revenue-generating activities.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between the social value of R&D and how much of that value the company doing it can capture. A discovery might benefit consumers, other firms, or researchers who build on it, and the original developer generally doesn’t get paid for all those benefits. So even if automating R&D would be enormously valuable to society, that doesn’t automatically imply an equally strong commercial incentive to do it.

For AI labs, though, improving AI itself is a particularly attractive kind of R&D to automate. If a lab can use its models to accelerate its own research, it can potentially develop better models, lower its costs, and gain an advantage over competitors. There’s a fairly direct route from the research to a private payoff.

So I’d expect incentives to be uneven. Labs might invest heavily in automating AI research while investing less in other kinds of research with very large social benefits but weaker opportunities to capture the returns. The question isn’t just how valuable the research is; it’s who receives that value and whether the lab can turn it into revenue or a competitive advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says developers do not get paid for all the benefits of R&D, so its social value does not automatically create an equally strong commercial incentive.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AI research with other research in terms of private payoff, but does not state that software R&D captures more value than biology R&D or basic research.

r003.rationale: It mentions revenue and competitive advantage, but does not identify financing further AI investment as a reason labs prioritize revenue-generating activities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between the social value of R&D and how much of that value the company doing the research can capture. Research can have enormous spillovers: you discover something, and other people build on it, consumers get better products, and competing firms learn from what you’ve done. Those benefits don’t all show up as revenue for the original researcher. So the social return can be much larger than the private return.

For AI labs, though, automating R&D has a particularly direct private benefit. If you can use your models to improve your next generation of models, you can potentially lower your costs, accelerate progress, and get ahead of competitors. You don’t need to capture the whole social value of research for that to be a very attractive investment.

So I wouldn’t infer that, because R&D is socially valuable, labs will automate the kinds of research that are most socially valuable. Their incentives are to automate research where they can capture the returns, especially research that improves their own AI systems. Those two things can overlap substantially, but they’re different objectives.

r001.rationale: It says research spillovers mean benefits do not all become revenue for the original researcher, so the social return can exceed the private return.

r002.rationale: It does not compare how much value labs can capture from software R&D versus biology R&D or basic research.

r003.rationale: It mentions cost reductions and competitive advantage from automating R&D, but does not say labs prioritize revenue-generating activities to finance further AI investment.
